implementation_notes: The standard library's realization without an executor: std::thread::spawn(f) starts the closure on a new OS thread and returns JoinHandle<T> immediately - the pattern's handle - and join() is the collect step, blocking until the thread finishes and returning Ok(value) or Err(payload) when the worker panicked. Values travel back either through that return value or through a channel (std::sync::mpsc, or a oneshot from an async runtime), which is the idiomatic replacement for the callback role: the receiver is handed to whoever collects. The handle is also the ownership token - dropping it detaches the thread and makes both result and panic unreachable - so the pattern's ownership rule is enforced by the type system rather than by convention. Blocking threads scale worse than an async runtime and cannot be cancelled or timed out, so this variant suits bounded pools and CPU-bound work; the async/await variant suits many outstanding I/O-bound calls.
pitfalls: join() folds the value and a panic into one Result: a panicking worker is not re-raised automatically, so the Err payload must be handled or the failure is lost.
Dropping a JoinHandle detaches the thread - its result and panic become unreachable, which is the pattern's silent-loss anti-pattern in Rust form.
The closure must be Send + 'static: borrowing caller state across the call does not compile, so shared data needs move, Arc or a channel.
std::thread offers no timeout and no cancellation; both require channels with recv_timeout or an async runtime.

variants.name: async fn futures with an executor (tokio::spawn)
variants.implementation_notes: Since async/await (Rust 1.39) the deferred call is the future itself: calling an async fn does nothing but build a state machine, awaiting it runs it, and the executor decides when and where - tokio::spawn(future) starts running the future in the background immediately and returns JoinHandle<T>, whose await yields Result<T, JoinError>, and whose abort() is the cancellation step. Futures are lazy and single-shot, which makes the pattern's semantics explicit: a future that is never polled performs no work (so fire-and-forget requires spawning) and a future cannot be run twice. Composition happens through combinators and join!/try_join!/select!, the closest idiomatic equivalent of the callback role, while channels (oneshot, mpsc) carry results out of tasks that were spawned for their side effects. Use this variant for many concurrent I/O-bound calls; keep the thread variant for bounded CPU work and for code that must not depend on a runtime.
pitfalls: A future that is never awaited or spawned does nothing at all - the most common Rust version of the silent no-op.
spawn requires Send + 'static: holding a non-Send value across an await boundary fails to compile, and shared state must be Arc/Mutex-based.
A runtime shutdown drops outstanding tasks without waiting: work can be discarded mid-flight unless the runtime is shut down gracefully or tasks are joined.
Blocking calls inside an async task occupy the executor thread and can starve every other task; wrap them in spawn_blocking.
JoinError conflates panic and cancellation, so error reporting must inspect it rather than treat all join failures alike.
